results.summary: This project implements an integrate-and-fire neuron model in Verilog. It accepts an 8-bit input current via the ui pins and produces a spike on uio[0] and the membrane potential on the uo pins. The neuron fires a spike when the membrane potential exceeds a threshold, without leakage or time-dependent dynamics. It is a simple demonstration intended for educational purposes, tested by applying different input currents and observing the firing rate.

This design plays the Super Mario Bros. theme tune on a piezo speaker using differential PWM modulation. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and outputs a differential sound wave on uo[0] and uo[1]. The design requires an external piezo speaker connected across those pins, and is tested by providing a 100 kHz clock and pulsing the reset pin. The project demonstrates a simple method for generating music from a hardware description language.

This design displays a 12-hour analog clock rendered with triangles using a race-the-beam technique on a 640x480 VGA output. It requires an external Tiny VGA interface and a 31.5 MHz clock, and accepts buttons to advance the hour and minute hands. The triangle coordinates are stored in a table and the rendering equations are recalculated during the vertical blanking interval by a small state machine. Debug pins allow inspection of internal variables, and a software model in Rust is provided for understanding.

This project displays the Caravel mask revision on a 7-segment display and outputs the lower 8 bits on bidirectional pins. It uses the ui pins as an index to cycle through the mask revision number in hexadecimal, LSB-first. The design is intended for testing and identification purposes, requiring no external hardware beyond the display. It is a simple utility block for the Openframe/Caravel platform.

This is a Verilog replica of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, a classic 3-voice chip used in 8-bit computers and consoles. It features three square wave tone generators, a noise generator, and an envelope generator, and is controlled via a multiplexed data/address bus. It provides both PWM and digital 8-bit audio outputs, and requires external hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker to be heard. The design is well-documented with a test suite and aims for hardware preservation and education.

This design implements a parallel cellular automaton based on Rule 110, capable of running over 200 cells in parallel each clock cycle. It provides a read/write bus to inspect and modify cell states, with addresses for blocks of 8 cells. The automaton can be halted and resumed, and is intended for exploring complex behavior, pseudo-random number generation, and computation. It requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout interface.

This project is a Verilog replica of the SN76489 programmable sound generator, a classic chip used in many 8-bit systems. It includes three square wave tone generators and a noise generator with programmable attenuation, and is controlled via an 8-bit data bus. It outputs both PWM and digital audio, and requires external hardware such as a DAC or low-pass filter and speaker for playback. The design is parameterized to match various SN76489 family variants and includes a comprehensive test suite.

This design implements a 3-layer spiking neural network with on-chip weights. It accepts an 8-bit input bus and control signals for execution and synchronization, and outputs the states of 8 neurons from the last layer. The documentation is minimal, with only a brief description and a truncated test instruction. It likely requires a host to provide inputs and control signals for operation.

This project implements an analog emulation monosynth with two oscillators and a second-order filter. It is controlled by writing to configuration registers via an 8-bit data bus and a 4-bit address bus, and provides both PWM and 8-bit digital audio outputs. The PWM output requires external filtering, and caution is advised when connecting to audio equipment. The documentation is incomplete, with register descriptions and oscillator/filter details marked as TODO.

This is a hardware implementation of the Simon Says memory game. The game uses four buttons and four LEDs to display a growing sequence of colors, each with a corresponding tone played on a speaker. It also supports a two-digit 7-segment display for showing the score. The design requires an external 50 kHz clock and is documented with wiring instructions, including a Wokwi online simulation for reference.
